claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A multi-fidelity surrogate can integrate hierarchical-interface and chemical-fluctuation descriptors with a limited amount of first-principles and CALPHAD calibration data.
The proposed surrogate can reliably predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical phase distributions, interfaces, and chemical fluctuations mediate load transfer and deformation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Chemical ordering or short-range order can alter dislocation mobility and strengthening behavior.
Representative-volume-element descriptors can capture the local and mesoscale effects responsible for elastic, plastic, and fracture behavior.
Training on a limited high-fidelity dataset bypasses the need for extensive full-scale computations.
The surrogate will predict all three target properties to within ±20% of experimental measurements.
The surrogate will reduce simulation time by approximately 5–10 times relative to conventional full-scale methods.
Exhaustive first-principles calculations, extensive CALPHAD simulations, and full-scale machine-learning models have high computational demands for this prediction task.
The method is intended for ambient and moderately elevated temperatures at which the hierarchical microstructure remains preserved.
Temperature and loading conditions can change phase state, chemical ordering, and mechanical response in high-entropy alloys.
The surrogate may become unreliable if phase separation, interface degradation, or chemical reordering makes its microstructural descriptors unrepresentative.
The surrogate may become unreliable when the scale of chemical fluctuations lies substantially outside the training distribution.
Processing and testing variability may cause prediction errors exceeding ±20%.
A benchmark using more than 10 specimens will falsify the hypothesis if any target property's prediction error exceeds ±20% or if speedup is below fivefold.
